Empirical Research Plan  
“UI Potential Duration, Labor‐Market Cycles, and Moral-Hazard Costs”

------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
------------------------------------------------------------------
Primary design: Sharp Regression-Discontinuity Design (RDD) around the statutory age thresholds that generate discontinuous jumps in potential UI duration (12→18, 18→22, 22→26 months).  
Why RDD?  
• Exact birth dates are observed, so age in days is measured without error.  
• Eligibility jumps deterministically at the cutoff, while everything else evolves smoothly with age.  
• German rules are constant across calendar time, so the same discontinuities are available in every macro state.  
Extension: “Difference-in-Discontinuities” (DiD-in-RDD).  Interact the RDD treatment indicator with a dummy for Recession (= national unemployment rate in the calendar quarter above long-run mean, or negative GDP growth).  This allows the size of the local jump to differ between booms and busts and answers whether moral-hazard costs vary with the cycle.

------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control  
------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
T_i = 1 if claimant’s exact age at UI start ≥ statutory cutoff k (42, 44, 49 before 4/1999; 45, 47, 52 after).  
Control group  
Claimants just below the same cutoff (|Age_i – k| ≤ h).  
Treatment timing / event date  
Event date = first day of UI claim.  Running variable  
Running_i = Age-in-days at the claim start.  Cutoffs: k_1, k_2, k_3 (adjust calendar-date-specific values after 1999 reform).  
We also use the jump in potential benefit months (PD_i) as an instrument for actual benefit duration (ABD_i) in a fuzzy-RDD 2SLS.

------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Continuity of potential outcomes in age absent the policy.  
 Plausibility: health, human-capital and demand factors evolve smoothly by single days around age 42/44/49.  
A2. No precise manipulation of the running variable (cannot misreport birth date).  
 Plausibility: birthdays are administratively certified and fixed.  
A3. Stable policy schedule—no other programs change discretely at the same ages.  
 Plausibility: no German social program has cliffs at these exact ages in 1987–2004.  
A4. Local integration of labor markets so macro shocks do not differentially affect workers within a few months of age.  
 Plausibility: within-cohort similarity over ±6 months is high.  
A5. For the 2SLS, monotonicity: crossing the cutoff weakly increases actual benefit duration for everyone (no defiers).  
 Plausibility: longer entitlement cannot shorten use.

------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats & Mitigation  
------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Differential previous labor-market history or tenure at cutoffs (older claimants have slightly longer career length).  
 Fix: show covariate continuity plots; control flexibly for tenure, wage, occupation in the RDD polynomial.  
T2. Age-specific labor-demand shocks (e.g., early retirement buy-outs aimed at 49+).  
 Fix: add industry×calendar-year fixed effects, exclude mass-layoff spells as robustness, use narrow bandwidth (≤6 months).  
T3. 1999 reform shifts cutoffs → potential contamination when pooling years.  
 Fix: estimate separate RDDs pre- and post-reform; difference-in-discontinuity design uses the shift as an additional DiD check.

------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline  
------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Libraries
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast high-dimensional OLS/2SLS
library(rdrobust)    # RDD estimation
library(AER)         # ivreg robustness

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Load and prep data
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
spells <- fread("UI_spells.csv")  # ~2 million spells

## Key variables
spells[, birth_date := as.IDate(birth_date)]
spells[, claim_date := as.IDate(claim_date)]
spells[, age_days  := as.numeric(claim_date - birth_date)]
spells[, age_years := age_days/365.25]

## Identify statutory cutoffs that apply on claim date
spells[, cutoff_age := fifelse(claim_date < "1999-04-01",
                               fifelse(age_years < 42, 42,
                               fifelse(age_years < 44, 44, 49)),
                               fifelse(age_years < 45, 45,
                               fifelse(age_years < 47, 47, 52)))]

## Treatment indicator
spells[, treat := (age_years >= cutoff_age)]

## Running var centred
spells[, running := age_days - cutoff_age*365.25]

## Outcomes
spells[, nonemp_months := pmin(as.numeric(next_job_date - claim_date)/30.4, 36)]
spells[, abd_months    := actual_benefit_duration/30.4]   # from admin data
spells[, exhausted     := (abd_months >= potential_duration_months)]

## Cycle indicator
macro <- fread("macro_series_quarterly.csv")              # GDP, U-rate
spells[, qdate := as.yearqtr(claim_date)]
spells <- merge(spells, macro, by="qdate", all.x=TRUE)
spells[, recession := (nat_unemp_rate > mean(nat_unemp_rate))]

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Sharp RDD: ITT on nonemployment months
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
bw <- 180  # +/- 6 months
sample_rdd <- spells[abs(running) <= bw]

r_it <- rdrobust(y = sample_rdd$nonemp_months,
                 x = sample_rdd$running,
                 c = 0, p = 1,
                 covs = sample_rdd[,.(gender, tenure_months, prewage)])

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Fuzzy RDD 2SLS: treat -> abd_months -> outcome
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# First stage and second stage in fixest
fs <- feols(abd_months ~ treat + poly(running,2) | 0, data = sample_rdd)
ss <- feols(nonemp_months ~ 1 | treat + poly(running,2), 
            instruments = ~ treat, data = sample_rdd)
etable(fs,ss)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Difference-in-Discontinuity: heterogeneity by cycle
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
sample_rdd[, treat_rec := treat*recession]
di_rdd <- feols(nonemp_months ~ treat + treat_rec + recession + poly(running,2),
                vcov = "HC1", data = sample_rdd)
etable(di_rdd)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Robustness: narrower bandwidth 90 days
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
sample90 <- spells[abs(running) <= 90]
r_90 <- rdrobust(sample90$nonemp_months, sample90$running, c=0)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results  
------------------------------------------------------------------
• ITT: crossing the first jump (12→18 months) should increase average non-employment duration by ≈ 1–1.5 weeks (0.25–0.35 months) – roughly 4–6% of the baseline spell length.  
• 2SLS LATE: an additional potential benefit month (6 extra weeks) likely raises nonemployment by ~0.15–0.20 month (elasticity ~0.25-0.30).  
• We expect the nonemployment response to be smaller in recessions because job-finding rates are low for everyone (search disincentives are less binding) → interaction coefficient negative.  
• Benefit exhaustion should fall sharply at the thresholds, with larger drops in recessions (more “insurance value”).

------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (RDD)  
C1: No manipulation of running variable …………………… 1  
C2: Covariate balance at cutoff ………………………………… 1  
C3: Continuity of potential outcomes ………………………… 0.8 (age-related health?)  
C4: Appropriate bandwidth / functional form ……………… 0.8  
C5: No spillovers / general equilibrium effects …………… 0.7  
Overall ≈ 4.3 / 5 → credible but must document robustness.

------------------------------------------------------------------
This plan exploits precise statutory age cliffs to obtain causal estimates of UI potential duration effects and how they vary with macro conditions, using Germany’s rich administrative data.
